questions.problem:
Consider the function $f(x,y)$ and the region $D$ given by

$$
f(x,y)=2x+2y,\,D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 2}.
$$

According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b)\in D$ such that the volume of the solid enclosed between the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and the $xy$-plane over the region $D$ equals the volume of the right cylinder with base $D$ and height $f(a,b).$ Find $a$ given that $b=2.$
questions.worked_solution:
According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b)\in D$ such that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A=f(a,b)\cdot \text{Area}(D).
$$

Evaluating the integral on the left-hand side, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}(2x+2y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}(2x+2y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[2xy+{y}^{2}]_{y=0}^{y=2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(4x+4)\,\text{d}x \\  & =[2{x}^{2}+4x]_{x=0}^{x=2} \\  & =(2\cdot {2}^{2}+4\cdot 2)-0 \\  & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\text{Area}(D)=2\cdot 2=4.
$$

Also, we are told that $b=2.$ So, our initial equation simplifies to

$$
\begin{aligned}16 & =f(a,2)\cdot 4 \\ 16 & =(2a+2\cdot 2)\cdot 4 \\ 4 & =2a+4 \\ 0 & =2a \\ a & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $(0,2)\in D.$ Therefore, the answer is $a=0.$

questions.problem:
Consider the function $f(x,y)$ and the region $D$ given by

$$
f(x,y)=x+y,\,D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 3,\,0\le y\le 3}.
$$

According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b)\in D$ such that the volume of the solid enclosed between the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and the $xy$-plane over the region $D$ equals the volume of the right cylinder with base $D$ and height $f(a,b).$ Find $b$ given that $a=2.$
questions.worked_solution:
According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b)\in D$ such that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A=f(a,b)\cdot \text{Area}(D).
$$

Evaluating the integral on the left-hand side, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}(x+y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}(x+y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}[xy+\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]_{y=0}^{y=3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(3x+\frac{9}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =[\frac{3{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{9x}{2}]_{x=0}^{x=3} \\  & =(\frac{3\cdot (3)^{2}}{2}+\frac{9\cdot (3)}{2})-0 \\  & =27.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\text{Area}(D)=3\cdot 3=9.
$$

Also, we are told that $a=2.$ So, our initial equation simplifies to

$$
\begin{aligned}27 & =f(2,b)\cdot 9 \\ 27 & =(2+b)\cdot 9 \\ 27 & =9b+18 \\ 9 & =9b \\ b & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $(2,1)\in D.$ Therefore, the answer is $b=1.$

questions.problem:
Consider the function $f(x,y)$ and the region $D$ given by

$$
f(x,y)={x}^{2}+2y+1,\,D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 3}.
$$

According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b)\in D$ such that the volume of the solid enclosed between the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and the $xy$-plane over the region $D$ equals the volume of the right cylinder with base $D$ and height $f(a,b).$ Find $b$ given that $a=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b)\in D$ such that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A=f(a,b)\cdot \text{Area}(D).
$$

Evaluating the integral on the left-hand side, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+2y+1)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}({x}^{2}+2y+1)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[{x}^{2}y+{y}^{2}+y]_{y=0}^{y=3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(3{x}^{2}+12)\,\text{d}x \\  & =[{x}^{3}+12x]_{x=0}^{x=2} \\  & =({2}^{3}+12\cdot 2)-0 \\  & =32.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\text{Area}(D)=2\cdot 3=6.
$$

Also, we are told that $a=1.$ So, our initial equation simplifies to

$$
\begin{aligned}32 & =f(1,b)\cdot 6 \\ 32 & =({1}^{2}+2b+1)\cdot 6 \\ 32 & =12b+12 \\ 20 & =12b \\ b & =\frac{5}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $(1,\frac{5}{3})\in D.$ Therefore, the answer is $b=\frac{5}{3}.$

questions.problem:
Consider the function $f(x,y)$ and the region $D$ given by

$$
f(x,y)=2x+4y,\,D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 2x}.
$$

According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b)\in D$ such that the volume of the solid enclosed between the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and the $xy$-plane over the region $D$ equals the volume of the right cylinder with base $D$ and height $f(a,b).$ Find $a$ given that $b=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b)\in D$ such that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A=f(a,b)\cdot \text{Area}(D).
$$

Evaluating the integral on the left-hand side, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}(2x+4y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2x}(2x+4y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[2xy+2{y}^{2}]_{y=0}^{y=2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}12{x}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =[4{x}^{3}]_{x=0}^{x=2} \\  & =32.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2x}\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[y]_{y=0}^{y=2x}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[{x}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=2} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we are told that $b=1.$ So, our initial equation simplifies to

$$
\begin{aligned}32 & =f(a,1)\cdot 4 \\ 32 & =(2a+4\cdot 1)\cdot 4 \\ 8 & =2a+4 \\ 4 & =2a \\ a & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $(2,1)\in D.$ Therefore, the answer is $a=2.$

questions.problem:
Consider the function $f(x,y)$ and the region $D$ given by

$$
f(x,y)=6{x}^{2}-2y+2,\,D={(x,y)\,:\,-1\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1}.
$$

According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b)\in D$ such that the volume of the solid enclosed between the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and the $xy$-plane over the region $D$ equals the volume of the right cylinder with base $D$ and height $f(a,b).$ Find $b$ given that $a=\frac{1}{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b)\in D$ such that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A=f(a,b)\cdot \text{Area}(D).
$$

Evaluating the integral on the left-hand side, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}(6{x}^{2}-2y+2)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(6{x}^{2}-2y+2)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}[6{x}^{2}y-{y}^{2}+2y]_{y=0}^{y=1}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(6{x}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =[2{x}^{3}+x]_{x=-1}^{x=1} \\  & =(2\cdot {1}^{3}+1)-(2\cdot (-1)^{3}+(-1)) \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\text{Area}(D)=1\cdot 2=2.
$$

Also, we are told that $a=\frac{1}{2}.$ So, our initial equation simplifies to

$$
\begin{aligned}6 & =f(\frac{1}{2},b)\cdot 2 \\ 6 & =(6\cdot {(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-2b+2)\cdot 2 \\ 3 & =\frac{7}{2}-2b \\ -\frac{1}{2} & =-2b \\ b & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{4})\in D.$ Therefore, the answer is $b=\frac{1}{4}.$

questions.problem: Find the average value of the function $f(x,y)=2x+3{y}^{2}$ on the region $D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that 

$$
\text{Area}(D)=1\cdot 2=2.
$$

Applying the average value formula, we find that the average value of the function is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{\text{ave}} & =\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{∬}_{D}(2x+3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}(2x+3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}[2xy+{y}^{3}]_{y=0}^{y=2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(4x+8)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[2{x}^{2}+8x]_{x=0}^{x=1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\cdot {1}^{2}+8\cdot 1) \\  & =\frac{10}{2} \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the average value of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{3}+6{y}^{2}$ on the region $D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 1}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that 

$$
\text{Area}(D)=2\cdot 1=2.
$$

Applying the average value formula, we find that the average value of the function is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{\text{ave}} & =\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{∬}_{D}({x}^{3}+6{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{3}+6{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}[{x}^{3}y+2{y}^{3}]_{y=0}^{y=1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}({x}^{3}+2)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}+2x]}_{x=0}^{x=2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{{2}^{4}}{4}+2\cdot 2-0) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Average Value of a Function Over a Polar Region
questions.problem: Find the average value of the function $f(x,y)=x-y$ on the portion of the disk of radius $1$ centered at the origin, where $y\le 0.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's sketch our region $D:$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14081614/assets/95faae88fb4909a86492e45101419fe872aeb1cc2eeabde9cf773c8f71d31fff.png)

Notice that 

$$
\text{Area}(D)=\frac{1}{2}\cdot \pi \cdot {1}^{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

The average value of the function over a region $D$ is given by

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,\pi \le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

Using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}x-y\,dA & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ){\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\frac{1}{3}{[{r}^{3}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )({1}^{3}-{0}^{3})\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]_{\pi }^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[(\operatorname{sin}⁡2\pi +\operatorname{cos}⁡2\pi )-(\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi +\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi )] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(1-(-1)) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{2}{\pi }\cdot \frac{2}{3}=\frac{4}{3\pi }.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Average Value of a Function Over a Polar Region
questions.problem: Find the average value of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}$ on the portion of the disk of radius $3$ centered at the origin, where $x\le 0.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's sketch our region $D:$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14081614/assets/25c1f00e588ddaa130f854d9f4e9dfe9b1158d7952a01bae8108ea4b94d3c347.png)

Notice that 

$$
\text{Area}(D)=\frac{1}{2}\cdot \pi \cdot {3}^{2}=\frac{9\pi }{2}.
$$

The average value of the function over a region $D$ is given by

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2}}.
$$

Using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{2}{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+1}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{2r}{{r}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}[\operatorname{ln}⁡({r}^{2}+1)]_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡10-\operatorname{ln}⁡1)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡10{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡10[\theta ]_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡10(\frac{3\pi }{2}-\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\pi \operatorname{ln}⁡10.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{2}{9\pi }\cdot \pi \operatorname{ln}⁡10=\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡10}{9}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Average Value of a Function Over a Polar Region
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14081614/assets/f84a8fcd4ed668a6b94d5b084ade49dc8fc027feff4baea862e2feaf68221534.png)

Find the average value of the function $f(x,y)=y\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ on the semicircle shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that 

$$
\text{Area}(D)=\frac{1}{2}\cdot \pi \cdot {1}^{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

The average value of the function over a region $D$ is given by

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $1$ centered at 
$(-1,0).$

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write the $y=\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-2x}$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-2x} \\ {y}^{2} & =-{x}^{2}-2x \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =-2x \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} & =-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) & =-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2} & =-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2}+2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

Therefore, in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le -2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \pi }.
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}y\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\sqrt{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {\int }_{0}^{-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta [\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]_{0}^{-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ((-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{4}-{0}^{4})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }16\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{4}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{[-\frac{{cos}^{5}⁡\theta }{5}]}_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =-\frac{4}{5}({cos}^{5}⁡\pi -{cos}^{5}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{(\frac{\pi }{2})}\cdot \frac{4}{5}=\frac{8}{5\pi }.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Average Value of a Function Over a Polar Region
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14081614/assets/719f86db69489f62bcbe2753e88cdc6713f04dc6f53415cc2484e2eaab8ffac3.png)

Find the average value of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{x}{y}$ on the semicircle shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that 

$$
\text{Area}(D)=\frac{1}{2}\cdot \pi \cdot {1}^{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

The average value of the function over a region $D$ is given by

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $1$ centered at 
$(0,1).$

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write the $x=\sqrt{2y-{y}^{2}}$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\sqrt{2y-{y}^{2}} \\ {x}^{2} & =2y-{y}^{2} \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =2y \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} & =2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) & =2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2} & =2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2}-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$

Therefore, in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}}.
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{x}{y}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\int }_{0}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{[\frac{{r}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }(2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -0)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(-1-1) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{(\frac{\pi }{2})}\cdot 1=\frac{2}{\pi }.
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14081614/assets/fd1a5a140c3a2d430312d6f6ceeb21d6b7282119c8ec53365553ff845d8c64d5.png)

Find the average value of the function $f(x,y)=x\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ on the semicircle shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that 

$$
\text{Area}(D)=\frac{1}{2}\cdot \pi \cdot (\frac{1}{2})^{2}=\frac{\pi }{8}.
$$

The average value of the function over a region $D$ is given by

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $\frac{1}{2}$ centered at 
$(0,-\frac{1}{2}).$

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write the $x=\sqrt{-{y}^{2}-y}$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\sqrt{-{y}^{2}-y} \\ {x}^{2} & =-{y}^{2}-y \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =-y \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} & =-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) & =-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2} & =-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2}+r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$

Therefore, in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 0}.
$$

Using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}x\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\sqrt{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {\int }_{0}^{-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta [\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]_{0}^{-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ((-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{4}-{0}^{4})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{4}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{[\frac{{sin}^{5}⁡\theta }{5}]}_{-\pi /2}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{20}({sin}^{5}⁡(0)-{sin}^{5}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{20}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{(\frac{\pi }{8})}\cdot \frac{1}{20}=\frac{2}{5\pi }.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding Points That Satisfy the Mean Value Theorem
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the function $f(x,y)$ and the region $D$ given by

$$
f(x,y) =\dfrac{xy}2, \qquad
D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 2y, \: 0 \leq y \leq 4 \big\}.
$$

According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b) \in D$ such that the volume of the solid enclosed between the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and the $xy$-plane over the region $D$ equals the volume of the right cylinder with base $D$ and height $f(a,b).$ Find $a$ given that $b=2.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b) \in D$ such that

$$
\iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A = f(a,b) \cdot \textrm{Area}(D).
$$

Evaluating the integral on the left-hand side, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}\frac{xy}{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{2y}\frac{xy}{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}[\frac{{x}^{2}y}{4}]_{x=0}^{x=2y}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =[\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}]_{y=0}^{y=4} \\  & =64.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{2y}\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}[x]_{x=0}^{x=2y}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}2y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[{y}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=4} \\  & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we are told that $b=2.$ So, our initial equation simplifies to

$$
\begin{aligned}64 & =f(a,2)\cdot 16 \\ 64 & =\frac{a\cdot 2}{2}\cdot 16 \\ 64 & =16a \\ a & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\left( 4,2 \right) \in D.$ Therefore, the answer is $a = 4.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Average Value of a Function
canonical_examples.problem: Find the average value of the function $f(x,y) = xy$ on the region $D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: -1 \leq x \leq 2, \: x \leq y \leq 3x \big\}$ given that the area of the region is $3$ square units.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Applying the average value formula, we find that the average value of the function is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{\text{ave}} & =\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{∬}_{D}xy\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{x}^{3x}xy\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{-1}^{2}[\frac{x{y}^{2}}{2}]_{y=x}^{y=3x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{-1}^{2}4{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[{x}^{4}]_{x=-1}^{x=2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(16-1) \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Average Value of a Function Over a Polar Region
canonical_examples.problem: Find the average value of the function $f(x,y) = 15xy^2$ on the portion of the disk of radius $1$ centered at the origin, where $x\geq 0,$ and $y \leq 0.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, let's sketch our region $D\mathbin{:}$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14081614/assets/a381fede820f9fc5ba08bb9569906d41a3e8f779de38b446c4f271ceef3a5ccd.png)

Notice that 

$$
\textrm{Area}(D) = \dfrac{1}{4} \cdot \pi \cdot 1^2 = \dfrac\pi 4.
$$

The average value of the function over a region $D$ is given by

$$
f_{\textrm{ave}} = \dfrac{1}{\textrm{Area}(D)} \, \iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A.
$$

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

In polar coordinates $(r, \theta),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
\Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 1, \: \dfrac{3\pi}{2} \leq \theta \leq 2\pi\right\}.
$$

Using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}15x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}15r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot (r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}15{r}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta {\int }_{0}^{1}5{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,{[{r}^{5}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta ({1}^{5}-0)\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={[{sin}^{3}⁡\theta ]}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi } \\  & =({sin}^{3}⁡(2\pi )-{sin}^{3}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})) \\  & =(0-(-1)) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
f_{\textrm{ave}} = \dfrac{4}{\pi} \cdot 1 = \dfrac{4}{\pi}.
$$
